items.title: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431, aged 19
items.claim: What did Joan of Arc achieve before her execution?

options.text: Nothing — her story is later legend

She convinced Charles VII she had divine guidance, led French forces to relieve the siege of Orléans in May 1429, helped recover Reims and have Charles crowned (July 1429); captured by Burgundians, sold to the English, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431
She was a Burgundian general who switched sides
She was canonised within months of her death

items.reveal:
Joan was a peasant from Domrémy who claimed visions of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret from age 13. After persuading Charles's court at Chinon, she joined the relief of Orléans aged 17. The siege was lifted in nine days; Reims (the traditional coronation city) was retaken; Charles VII was crowned on 17 July 1429.

She was captured at Compiègne (May 1430), held for ransom by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and tried by a French ecclesiastical court at Rouen. The trial of 1455-56 (after the English left) annulled the conviction. She was canonised in 1920.

The Hundred Years War ended in French victory at Castillon (1453).
items.why: The Hundred Years War's turning point is a teenager with no military training. Joan of Arc's trial transcripts survive — she remains one of the most documented medieval figures and a case in how religion, war and gender intersect.

items.title: Henry VIII didn't divorce his first wife — he had the marriage annulled
items.claim: Henry VIII's first marriage ended in 1533. What is the technically correct description?

options.text: An annulment — Archbishop Cranmer declared the marriage to Catherine of Aragon had never been valid
A separation only, with Catherine retaining queenly status
A papal divorce granted by Clement VII

items.reveal:
Henry argued that his marriage to Catherine — his brother Arthur's widow — was barred by Leviticus 20:21. Cranmer's court at Dunstable in May 1533 declared the marriage void from the start.

The distinction matters: annulment says no marriage existed; divorce ends a valid one. Mary I's legitimacy depended on which view prevailed (the Second Act of Succession, 1536, made her illegitimate; the Third, 1543, restored her in line). Catherine refused to accept the annulment until her death in 1536.
items.why: The vocabulary of Tudor religion is technical. 'Divorce' makes it sound modern; 'annulment' shows it as a legal claim about the past — which is why the marriage to Anne could be valid at all.

items.title: The Spinning Jenny multiplied a worker's output eightfold
items.claim: What did James Hargreaves invent around 1764?

options.text: The Spinning Jenny — a multi-spindle frame allowing one operator to spin eight (later up to 120) threads at once; patented 1770, transformed cotton production

items.reveal:
Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver, named the device after his daughter (or wife) Jenny. Early versions had 8 spindles; later models up to 120. Cotton output per worker rose dramatically.

The jenny was joined by Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769, water-powered) and Samuel Crompton's mule (1779, combining both). Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) mechanised weaving. Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) mechanised seed-removal in the US South — increasing cotton supply and intensifying slavery.

Lancashire became the centre of world cotton manufacture by 1830, employing perhaps half a million workers by mid-century. Cotton's raw material came largely from the slave plantations of the US South until the American Civil War.
items.why: The Industrial Revolution was a sequence of specific machines invented by specific people, each enabling the next. 'Cotton' is shorthand for a chain of innovation that links Lancashire mills to plantation slavery.
